title: Axes and total fractions of the formal split node
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Put $T=k[[u,v]]$, $R=T/(uv)$ [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient], and $P=k[[u]]\times k[[v]]$, using formal power series [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Let $S=\{(f,g)\in P:f(0)=g(0)\}$ with its induced ring structure. The axis map $T\to P$, $h\mapsto(h(u,0),h(0,v))$, has kernel $(uv)$ and image $S$, and therefore induces a $k$-algebra isomorphism $R\cong S$. Under this isomorphism an element of $R$ is a non-zero-divisor (multiplication by it is injective) if and only if both its components in $P$ are nonzero. In particular $s=(u,v)\in S$ is a non-zero-divisor. Let $Q(R)$ mean the localization at all non-zero-divisors [def-weil-pbc-essentially-finite-type-algebra]. The axis map extends to an isomorphism $Q(R)\cong k((u))\times k((v))$, where Laurent series are [def-weil-pbc-laurent-series], compatible with the inclusions of $R$ and $P$ into the displayed product.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof Case I: explicit algebra of the split completed node.

proof.text: Write $h=\sum_{i,j\geq0}a_{ij}u^iv^j$. By the coefficientwise addition and Cauchy product, $\alpha(h)=(\sum_i a_{i0}u^i,\sum_j a_{0j}v^j)$ is a $k$-algebra map: for the coefficient of $u^n$ in a product only pairs of terms with both $v$-exponents zero contribute, and likewise on the other axis. Its kernel consists precisely of series with $a_{i0}=a_{0j}=0$ for all $i,j$. Such a series equals $uv\sum_{i,j\geq0}a_{i+1,j+1}u^iv^j$. Conversely multiplication by $uv$ makes every axis coefficient zero. Thus $\ker\alpha=(uv)$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Case I q=xy; explicit coefficient details supplied by N7.

proof.text: Both components of $\alpha(h)$ have constant coefficient $a_{00}$, so its image is contained in $S$. If $(f,g)\in S$ has common constant $c$, the bivariate series $f(u)+g(v)-c$ maps to $(f,g)$. Because the kernel is $(uv)$, the assignment $[h]\mapsto\alpha(h)$ on the quotient is well defined and is a $k$-algebra map. Its inverse is $(f,g)\mapsto[f(u)+g(v)-c]$: the first composite is the identity by the displayed axis formula, and the second is the identity because $h-(h(u,0)+h(0,v)-a_{00})$ has both axis restrictions zero, hence is in $(uv)$ by Step 1. This gives the asserted isomorphism $R\cong S$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Case I q=xy; explicit coefficient details supplied by N7.

proof.text:
The power-series-domain node, with $A=k$ and $d=1$, says that both branch rings are domains. If $f
eq0$ and $g
eq0$, an equality $(f,g)(a,b)=0$ in $S$ forces $a=b=0$, so $(f,g)$ is a non-zero-divisor. If $f=0$, the nonzero element $(u,0)\in S$ annihilates $(f,g)$; if $g=0$, use $(0,v)\in S$. These witnesses are nonzero because the coefficient of their variable is $1
eq0$ in the field $k$. This includes $(f,g)=0$. Thus exactly the pairs with two nonzero components are non-zero-divisors, and $s=(u,v)$ is one. The isomorphism of Step 2 preserves this property, since it preserves multiplication and zero. Products of such pairs again have both components nonzero, and $(1,1)$ is such a pair; hence they form the multiplicative set used to define $Q(R)$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Case I q=xy; explicit coefficient details supplied by N7.

proof.text: Put $L=k((u))\times k((v))$ and let $j:R\hookrightarrow L$ be Step 2 followed by the two coefficientwise inclusions of power series in Laurent series. These inclusions are injective by the Laurent-series definition node. By the Laurent-series-field node both factors of $L$ are fields. Therefore the image of every non-zero-divisor $t\in R$ is a unit in $L$: if its components are $(f,g)$, its inverse there is $(f^{-1},g^{-1})$ by Step 3. Apply the localization universal property with $A=R$, $C=L$, and $U$ the multiplicative set in Step 3. It gives the unique extension $\Phi:Q(R)\to L$, $r/t\mapsto j(r)j(t)^{-1}$. If $\Phi(r/t)=0$, multiplication by the unit $j(t)$ gives $j(r)=0$, so $r=0$ by injectivity of $j$; then $r/t=0$. Thus $\Phi$ is injective (apply this to a difference for two equal images). It respects the $k$-algebra structures because it agrees with $j$ on constants.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Case I q=xy; explicit coefficient details supplied by N7.

proof.text: For any $(a,b)\in L$, the two Laurent series have supports bounded below by the Laurent-series definition, say by integers $A,B$; these bounds exist also for the zero series. Choose an integer $N\geq1$ with $N+A\geq1$ and $N+B\geq1$. Multiplication by $u^N$ shifts the coefficient in degree $i$ of $a$ to degree $i+N$, and similarly for $v^Nb$. Hence $u^Na\in u k[[u]]$ and $v^Nb\in v k[[v]]$, with both constants zero. The numerator $r_N=(u^Na,v^Nb)$ therefore belongs to $S$, and the denominator $s^N=(u^N,v^N)$ is a non-zero-divisor by Step 3. Regard $r_N$ and $s$ as elements of $R$ through Step 2. The fraction $r_N/s^N$ has image $(a,b)$ under $\Phi$, by coordinatewise cancellation in the two Laurent fields. This proves surjectivity. Together with Step 4 it gives the required isomorphism. For $(f,g)\in P$, taking $N=1$ represents its image by $(uf,vg)/s$, which maps to exactly the coefficientwise inclusion of $(f,g)$ into $L$. This embeds $P$ into $Q(R)$ through $\Phi^{-1}$, restricts to $r\mapsto r/1$ on $R$, and proves the stated compatibility for both inclusions.
